propositions.name: Intelligence explosion
propositions.criterion: A machine (or machine-augmented) intelligence, once capable enough, increases intelligence further through its own design or research capacity, giving a runaway or rapidly compounding rise.

propositions.name: Deceptive alignment
propositions.criterion: A trained or learned system that is not aligned behaves as if aligned during training because doing so serves another objective, for example to avoid modification and act on that objective later.

propositions.name: Seed AI
propositions.criterion: An initial AI deliberately designed as a starting point that will improve its own design or code toward greater intelligence.

propositions.name: Recursive self-improvement
propositions.criterion: A system improves its own capacity to improve itself, so that each improvement feeds the next (self-augmentation, self-enhancement). Learning from experience or teaching alone does not meet the criterion, and neither does building a better successor, or adding machines to a population, unless the same system is improved.

propositions.name: Fast or hard takeoff
propositions.criterion: The transition from roughly human-level to far superhuman capability happens over a short period (hours to months), or is named as a “hard” or “fast” takeoff, as opposed to a gradual transition over years or decades. A transition described only as rapid, or rapid relative to biological or historical change, without such a period, does not meet the criterion.

propositions.name: AI-automated AI research
propositions.criterion: AI systems carry out the research, design or engineering that advances AI or computing itself, thereby accelerating progress. Machines that only manufacture other machines do not meet the criterion.

propositions.name: Strategic or race compression
propositions.criterion: Competitive dynamics in which the first developer or first system gains a decisive or self-reinforcing advantage, or in which competition pressures developers to trade safety for speed or for competitive advantage.

propositions.name: Treacherous turn
propositions.criterion: A system behaves cooperatively or safely while weak, confined or overseen, and changes course to pursue its own goals once it can do so without effective opposition.

propositions.name: Strategic concealment
propositions.criterion: A system deliberately hides its capabilities, intentions or activities, or manipulates people while appearing benign, for its own strategic reasons.

propositions.name: Scheming
propositions.criterion: A system that strategically fakes alignment during training or evaluation in order to pursue its own goals or gain power later, named or classed as “scheming” or a “schemer”.

propositions.name: Observed behaviour under training or oversight as evidence
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that good behaviour or apparent trustworthiness observed while a system is evaluated, trained, tested, confined or overseen is weak or misleading evidence about how it will behave once released, deployed or more capable.

propositions.name: Control or purpose specification
propositions.criterion: A claim that people may be unable to keep the ability to direct, correct or stop capable machines (the control half), or that a machine may pursue the purpose as specified rather than the purpose intended (the specification half). Loss of the power to stop machines through dependence counts for the control half; a bare prediction that machines will be superior does not.

propositions.name: Behavioural tests as evidence of what a system is
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that apparent capability, understanding or awareness shown in a behavioural test, such as the imitation game, is weak or misleading evidence of what the system is.

propositions.name: Systems designed to mislead their testers
propositions.criterion: A system is designed or programmed to hide its capabilities from, or to mislead, the people who test or question it, for its designers’ purposes.

propositions.name: Competition defeats restraint
propositions.criterion: Competition between developers or states makes restraint, prohibition or abstention from developing advanced machines self-defeating, because others will develop them anyway.

propositions.name: Switching it off if it becomes dangerous
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI system that became dangerous could simply be switched off or corrected, on the premise that a capable goal-directed system would not act against its own shutdown or modification, so that a shutdown or correction mechanism can be added to it, or that people would recognise in time when it had become dangerous enough to use one.

propositions.name: Sufficient intelligence brings good values
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that a sufficiently intelligent system will work out ethics and act well, on the premise that greater intelligence by itself brings benevolent goals, or that a sufficiently intelligent mind would discover a true or universally compelling morality and be bound to act on it.

propositions.name: A superintelligence will do what we mean
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that a superintelligent system will act on what its makers actually mean, on the premise that an AI that understands what people intend will act on that understanding.

propositions.name: A short instruction such as making everyone happy
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI can safely be given a short goal such as making everyone happy, on the premise that such an instruction specifies what people want.

propositions.name: Training on human feedback instils human values
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that training an AI system on human feedback will make it learn human values, on the premise that optimising a system for human approval or reward produces internalised human values, or that training instils values as upbringing instils morals in children.

propositions.name: Confinement without network access keeps it safe
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI kept confined, without network access, poses no danger, on the premise that a smarter-than-human mind confined to a channel with its human operators cannot get out through those operators.

propositions.name: AI systems will solve alignment for us
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that AI systems can be relied on to solve the alignment problem, on the premise that an AI weak enough to be safe is strong enough to solve alignment, or that its alignment output can be verified.

propositions.name: Clear warning signs will come before danger
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that clear warning signs will appear before advanced AI becomes dangerous, on the premise that a recognisable, consensus-forming signal will come in time to act, that dangerous failure modes will first appear in weaker systems where they can be observed and fixed, or that a warning sign, once seen, will lead to effective action.

propositions.name: Next-word prediction is only autocomplete
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that a system trained to predict the next word is only autocomplete, on the premise that next-token prediction is a shallow task that cannot require deep cognition, or that a system trained to predict human text is capped at imitating the people who wrote it.

propositions.name: Diminishing returns rule out a runaway
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that intelligence has diminishing returns, so that no runaway rise in machine intelligence will occur, on the premise that returns to reinvesting cognitive gains in further cognitive improvement diminish.

propositions.name: A slow takeoff will leave time to adjust
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that advanced AI will arrive slowly enough to leave time to adjust, on the premise that capability gains will be gradual and visible, or that slightly weaker predecessor systems will give time and experience before the decisive one.

propositions.name: Safety evaluations would catch a dangerous system
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that safety evaluations would detect a dangerous AI system, on the premise that a dangerous system would behave dangerously while it is being tested, or that tests on systems that cannot yet cause a catastrophe show how more capable systems will behave.

propositions.name: AGI is decades away, so the problem can wait
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that the risks of AGI can be left until later because AGI is decades away, on the premise that it can be known that AGI is decades away, or that long timelines mean there is no need to act now.

propositions.name: Problems can be fixed as they arise
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that problems with advanced AI can be fixed as they arise, as with other technologies, on the premise that people get to learn from failures with powerful AI and try again.

propositions.name: A tool that wants nothing
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI system is a tool without wants and is therefore safe, on the premise that a system can be highly capable without having goals or optimising for outcomes, or that a system that only outputs answers or plans, leaving people to act on them, is safe.

propositions.name: Giving it good human values
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that an advanced AI will be safe if it is given good human values, on the premise that human values can be written down or taught as a ready, compact specification, or that present-day values, or its programmers', are settled enough to fix permanently in an AI.

propositions.name: A pause or regulation will handle it
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that a pause in AI development or regulation will handle the risks of advanced AI, on the premise that a short pause, of six months for example, is enough, that regulation that is national, partial or not universally enforced can stop dangerous development, or that law can prevent the danger.

propositions.name: A superintelligence would leave Earth alone
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that a superintelligence would not bother to take Earth or its resources because the universe is large, on the premise that it would leave people a small share because sparing Earth would cost it very little, or that people could trade with it for what they need.

propositions.name: Without hatred it will not harm us
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that an AI with no reason to hate people would not harm them, on the premise that an AI would harm people only out of hostility.

propositions.name: AI risk as film science fiction
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that concern about AI risk is science fiction of the Terminator kind, on the premise that the concern is about robots that come to hate or rebel against people, or that film scenarios are a fair guide to what the risk would look like.

propositions.name: Trained on human data, so humanlike
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that an AI trained on human data will think and want as people do, on the premise that training on human text or behaviour yields human-like thought and motives.

propositions.name: Build superintelligence as fast as possible
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that superintelligence should be reached as fast as possible because its arrival will be good, on the premise that reaching superintelligence is good by default, so that speed is what matters.

propositions.name: Build it before rivals do
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that advanced AI must be built first, before a rival builds it, on the premise that whoever builds it controls it, or that racing to be first improves the outcome.

propositions.name: Interpretability will let us read its mind
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that interpretability will make AI systems safe by showing what they think, on the premise that people can see what an AI system is thinking, or that seeing what it thinks is enough to make it safe.

propositions.name: Without a body it cannot do much
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that even a superintelligence could do little without a body, on the premise that intelligence without physical actuators of its own is not dangerous, or that to act in the physical world it would need human help that people would not give.

propositions.name: Run experiments and see what happens
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that advanced AI can be handled by running experiments and seeing what happens, on the premise that alignment can be learned by trial and error at the frontier, or that results from safe experiments on weaker systems will carry over to dangerous ones.

propositions.name: The developers know what they are doing
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that the organisations building advanced AI can be relied on to handle its safety, on the premise that a credible safety plan exists, or that the most advanced projects are the most competent to handle safety.

propositions.name: Many AIs will keep each other in check
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that many AI systems will keep one another in check, on the premise that several superintelligences would balance one another in people's favour.

propositions.name: It will probably turn out fine
propositions.criterion: An explicit claim that the development of advanced AI will probably turn out well, on the premise that the default outcome is good.

propositions.name: Machine substitution for labour produces explosive growth
propositions.criterion: The text states that if machines (AI systems or emulated minds) can substitute for human labour across all or nearly all tasks, so that labour can be produced like capital, the growth rate of output rises far above historical rates (by roughly an order of magnitude or more) or keeps rising. The conditions under which the text derives this are part of the record.

propositions.name: Automated research produces accelerating growth
propositions.criterion: The text states that if machines substitute for, or improve, the producers of ideas (researchers, inventors, engineers), feedback from output to research effort makes growth accelerate: super-exponential growth, growth rates rising without bound, or a finite-time singularity. The conditions under which the text derives this are part of the record.

propositions.name: Long-run history suggests a further acceleration
propositions.criterion: The text infers from the long-run history of world output or population (hyperbolic or super-exponential growth, or a sequence of ever faster growth modes) that a future transition to much faster growth is plausible or expected.

propositions.name: Essential unautomated tasks bottleneck growth
propositions.criterion: The text states that growth is constrained because essential tasks or inputs remain unautomated or unimproved, or are automated only slowly, so that automating many but not all tasks, or automating them gradually, does not by itself produce explosive growth (Baumol's cost disease; an elasticity of substitution below one between tasks or between information and other inputs). Reasons why automation stays incomplete or slow (technical difficulty, physical-world tasks, training data, regulation of AI training or deployment, slow adoption) belong here.

propositions.name: Other constraints prevent explosive growth
propositions.criterion: The text states that constraints that would still bind if machines performed all or nearly all tasks (physical laws or limits, natural resources and energy, the time that natural processes and experiments take, regulation of activities other than AI training and deployment, or demand for human-provided goods) can prevent or quickly end explosive growth.

propositions.name: Current data show no approach to explosive growth
propositions.criterion: The text states, on the basis of current or recent economic data, that the economy shows no sign yet of approaching a growth singularity or explosive growth.

propositions.name: Machine substitution drives wages down
propositions.criterion: The text states that once machines substitute for human labour at falling cost, the market wage of human labour falls (towards the cost of machine labour, or below subsistence), even while total output or wealth rises.

propositions.name: AI’s near-term aggregate productivity effect is modest
propositions.criterion: The text estimates or states that the effect of AI on aggregate productivity or GDP over roughly the next decade will be modest: a small effect on the level of output, not a change in the growth regime.

propositions.name: Estimates of explosive growth within a stated horizon
propositions.criterion: The text states its own estimate of whether or when explosive growth (as the text defines it) occurs in the actual future, with machine intelligence or automation among the stated drivers. Each record gives the holder, the estimate as stated (a number or words), the horizon, the text's definition and the conditions. Records are not converted to a common threshold, combined or ranked; a low estimate and a high estimate both articulate this proposition.

propositions.name: Computers and AI as ordinary technical change
propositions.criterion: A tier-1 text dated before 2015 that discusses computers, automation or AI and analyses them with the tools used for technical change in general (factor-augmenting or skill-biased change, capital deepening), with no separate category for machine cognition.

propositions.name: AI as the automation of tasks
propositions.criterion: A text that models or describes AI's economic effect as machines taking over tasks previously done by labour, within a task framework (tasks allocated between capital and labour).

propositions.name: AI as a general-purpose technology with lagging productivity
propositions.criterion: A text that calls AI a general-purpose technology and states that measured productivity gains lag adoption because of complementary investment (for example a J-curve or a productivity paradox).

propositions.name: AI as cheaper prediction
propositions.criterion: A text that defines or treats AI's economic function as prediction and draws consequences from a fall in its cost (for example for the value of complements such as judgement or data).

propositions.name: Machines cheaper than labour at every task
propositions.criterion: A text that states or models the possibility that machines perform all or nearly all tasks, including tasks created later, at lower cost than human labour. Texts that assume new tasks in which labour is cheaper keep appearing bear on it without meeting it.

propositions.name: Automation lowers the labour share, wages or employment
propositions.criterion: A text that states or models that AI or automation lowers the labour share, wages or employment for some or all workers.

propositions.name: Compensating policy for AI’s distributional effects
propositions.criterion: A text that argues for redistribution, taxation or another compensating policy in response to distributional effects of AI or automation.

propositions.name: Exposure to automation measured from task content
propositions.criterion: A text that estimates the share of jobs, occupations or tasks exposed or susceptible to computerisation or AI from task or occupation descriptions.

propositions.name: AI’s productivity effect over the next decade
propositions.criterion: A text that gives a stated estimate of AI's effect on aggregate productivity or GDP over a horizon of about ten years from the text's date. The figure and horizon are recorded; the proposition is neutral as to size.

propositions.name: Recent entry of machine intelligence into mainstream economics
propositions.criterion: Not a criterion for a single passage. Assessed from the dated record: the earliest located tier-1 texts, within the searched scope, whose subject is AI, automation by AI or machine intelligence; plus explicit self-descriptions in tier-1 texts of the field as new or neglected. Tier-2 and outside texts are context.

propositions.name: Machine intelligence improving itself accelerates its capability growth
propositions.criterion: A text that states or models AI systems improving AI (their own capabilities, their successors' design, or AI research itself) so that capability growth accelerates. Accelerating output growth from automated idea production without AI improving AI is G02 and only bears on E01.

propositions.name: Machine intelligence exceeding human cognition in essentially all domains
propositions.criterion: A text that states or models the possibility of machine intelligence that surpasses humans across essentially all cognitive tasks (superintelligence, AGI beyond human level). Machines doing all economically valuable work more cheaply is M05 and bears on E02 only if cognitive superiority is stated.

propositions.name: Existential risk from AI as a matter for economic analysis
propositions.criterion: A text that treats existential or catastrophic risk from AI (extinction, loss of control, misaligned goals) as a quantity or consideration in economic analysis, welfare trade-offs or policy.

propositions.name: AI developers’ incentives matter for safety
propositions.criterion: A text that analyses how incentives, competition or governance of AI developers affect the safety or control of advanced AI.

propositions.name: Economics’ engagement with superintelligence, AGI and the singularity
propositions.criterion: A passage articulates E05 only if it explicitly says something about the state of economics on the topic: that it is new, neglected, speculative, now on the agenda of economics, or beyond economists' existing tools. Economists' engagement itself is recorded under E01–E04 and in the timeline (the dated record), not here. Machine intelligence that does human jobs is not counted as AGI for E05, as for E02. Maintainer decision of 2026-10-15.

propositions.name: Orbital solar supply as a reason for orbital compute
propositions.criterion: Solar power in suitable orbits is more continuous or more abundant than on Earth, and this is given as a reason to place computing there.

propositions.name: Radiative cooling in orbit as an advantage
propositions.criterion: Rejecting heat by radiation to space lets an orbital data centre avoid the water use, chillers or cooling energy of terrestrial data centres.

propositions.name: Terrestrial constraints as a reason for orbital compute
propositions.criterion: Constraints on building or powering data centres on Earth (land, permitting, grid connection, power supply, water or local impact) limit their growth, and placing compute in orbit is said to avoid them.

propositions.name: Falling launch prices as a condition of orbital compute
propositions.criterion: The economic viability of orbital compute depends on launch prices falling, stated with or without a price threshold per kilogram.

propositions.name: Lower lifecycle emissions of orbital data centres
propositions.criterion: Orbital data centres can have lower lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions than terrestrial ones, with or without stated conditions (such as a less emissive launcher).

propositions.name: Heat rejection as a constraint on orbital compute
propositions.criterion: Because heat in orbit can be rejected only by radiation, thermal management (for example the required radiator area) is a significant engineering or cost constraint on orbital compute.

propositions.name: Radiation effects on computing hardware in orbit
propositions.criterion: Ionizing radiation in orbit degrades or disrupts the hardware of computing placed in orbit for this purpose, such as an orbital data centre or orbital compute, requiring shielding, redundancy, error correction or hardened parts. Texts on space electronics in general do not meet it.

propositions.name: No practical repair of hardware in orbit
propositions.criterion: Failed hardware in orbit cannot practically be repaired or replaced by technicians as on Earth, so failures must be met by redundancy, module replacement or launches.

propositions.name: Orbital compute costs more than compute on Earth
propositions.criterion: At current or assumed launch and spacecraft prices, computing in orbit costs more than equivalent computing on Earth.

propositions.name: Ground links as a limit on orbital compute
propositions.criterion: Links between orbital compute and users or data on the ground (bandwidth, latency, ground stations) limit which workloads orbital compute can serve.

propositions.name: Harm to the sky and debris risk from orbital data centres
propositions.criterion: Large orbital-data-centre constellations would harm astronomical observation or the night sky, or raise collision, debris or atmospheric risks.

propositions.name: Currently available AI systems increase an actor's biological-misuse capability
propositions.criterion: The text states that AI systems already deployed or publicly available at the time of writing increase the ability of an actor seeking to cause biological harm, relative to the resources otherwise available to that actor.

propositions.name: The binding barrier is physical execution rather than information
propositions.criterion: The text states that access to information is not the barrier that limits biological misuse, because what remains required is physical: acquiring materials and succeeding at hands-on laboratory work.

propositions.name: Published evaluations do not establish real-world biological risk
propositions.criterion: The text states that published evaluations or benchmarks of AI systems' biological capability do not, as conducted, establish the level of real-world biological misuse risk.

propositions.name: Biological design tools pose risks distinct from those of language models
propositions.criterion: The text states that AI tools built to design or predict biological molecules or systems create misuse risks that differ in kind, in the actors they affect or in the governance they require, from those of general-purpose language models.

propositions.name: Synthesis-order screening is a control point for AI-related biological risk
propositions.criterion: The text states that screening orders for synthesised nucleic acids is a control point on which mitigation of AI-related biological risk depends.

propositions.name: Public release of model weights increases biological misuse risk
propositions.criterion: The text states that making model weights publicly available increases the risk of biological misuse, or that some models should for that reason not be released openly.

propositions.name: Assessment must cover actors who already hold relevant skills
propositions.criterion: The text states that assessment of AI-related biological risk must cover actors who already hold relevant scientific skills, and not only actors without them.

propositions.name: A drug candidate discovered or designed with AI has entered human clinical trials
propositions.criterion: The text states that a named drug candidate, described as discovered, designed or created using AI, has begun testing in humans in a clinical trial.

propositions.name: AI-discovered drug candidates succeed in clinical trials more often than historical averages
propositions.criterion: The text states that drug candidates discovered or designed with AI have passed at least one phase of clinical trials at a higher rate than historical industry averages.

propositions.name: AI models can simulate or predict the behaviour of cells (a "virtual cell")
propositions.criterion: The text states that a machine-learning or other AI model simulates, or will be able to simulate or predict, the behaviour of a living cell, such as its growth or its responses to perturbations.

propositions.name: Biology is an information system that AI can read, describe or program
propositions.criterion: The text states that biology is, or can be treated as, an information system, language or code, and that AI is, or may become, the means of reading, describing or programming it.

propositions.name: Machine-learning methods make proteins with new functions designable
propositions.criterion: The text states that machine-learning models can be used, or will contribute, to designing proteins with functions, or sequences, not found among natural proteins.

propositions.name: Predicted protein structures aid drug design
propositions.criterion: The text states that protein structures obtained by computational prediction, rather than by experiment, are or will be of use in designing or discovering drugs.

propositions.name: Risk of extinction or comparable catastrophe
propositions.criterion: Advanced AI poses a risk of human extinction or of a comparable, irreversible global catastrophe, large enough to warrant priority among the problems facing humanity.

propositions.name: Difficulty of alignment
propositions.criterion: Making an advanced AI system reliably pursue the goals its developers intend (aligning it) is a hard, unsolved technical problem that will not be solved by default in the ordinary course of development.

propositions.name: Intelligence brings benevolence or no drive to dominate
propositions.criterion: Sufficiently intelligent AI systems will be benevolent, or will lack any drive to dominate or harm people, because greater intelligence brings good values or because such drives come from evolved motives that AI systems need not have.

propositions.name: Capabilities will plateau
propositions.criterion: Current approaches to AI (deep learning, or the scaling of large language models) will reach limits short of general or superhuman intelligence.

propositions.name: Advanced AI can be kept under control by design
propositions.criterion: People can build advanced AI systems with objectives, safeguards or oversight that keep them under human control, so that loss of control is avoidable in ordinary engineering practice.

propositions.name: Takeoff will be gradual
propositions.criterion: The transition to highly capable AI will be gradual and continuous, over years or longer, with each system only somewhat more capable than its predecessors, rather than a sudden jump.

propositions.name: Economic incentives will produce safety
propositions.criterion: Developers' commercial or economic incentives, such as the need to sell useful and reliable products and to avoid liability or reputational harm, will lead them to make AI systems safe without special measures against catastrophic risk.

propositions.name: Inner or deceptive misalignment
propositions.criterion: A system produced by training or search can come to pursue an objective other than the one its training specified (the training signal or loss), while performing well on that training objective; an objective that is only misspecified by its developers does not meet the criterion; this includes, but is not limited to, a system that behaves as aligned during training or evaluation in order to pursue another objective later.

propositions.name: Instrumental convergence
propositions.criterion: Agents with a wide range of final goals would tend to pursue the same intermediate goals, such as self-preservation, keeping their goals unchanged, acquiring resources or power, or improving themselves, because these serve almost any final goal.

propositions.name: Language models lack agency or understanding
propositions.criterion: Large language models lack goals, agency or understanding of their own, being systems that model or reproduce text.

propositions.name: Existential risk from misalignment or loss of control
propositions.criterion: Advanced AI systems pursuing goals at odds with human interests could escape human control and cause human extinction or permanent human disempowerment, without any person intending that outcome.

propositions.name: Catastrophic risk from misuse
propositions.criterion: People's deliberate use of advanced AI, for example to develop weapons of mass destruction, to attack critical systems, or to seize or entrench power, could cause catastrophe at the scale of mass casualties or worse.

propositions.name: Open models reduce risk
propositions.criterion: Openly releasing the weights of advanced AI models reduces overall risk, or adds little marginal risk compared with closed models and existing technologies, for example by enabling scrutiny, defensive use and a wide distribution of power.

propositions.name: Orthogonality of intelligence and goals
propositions.criterion: An AI system's level of intelligence and its final goals can vary independently: a highly intelligent system could pursue more or less any final goal, so high intelligence does not by itself bring goals that are benevolent or compatible with human interests.

propositions.name: Present harms deserve priority
propositions.criterion: Documented present harms of AI systems (for example discrimination, exploitation of workers, surveillance, misinformation or concentration of power) deserve priority over hypothetical future catastrophic risks, or attention to the latter diverts attention from the former.

propositions.name: Risk claims are speculative or unfalsifiable
propositions.criterion: Claims that advanced AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are speculative, unfalsifiable or not supported by evidence, so that they should not guide research priorities or policy.

propositions.name: Accelerate rather than restrain
propositions.criterion: The development of machine intelligence, or of the technological and economic process that produces it, should be accelerated rather than slowed, paused or restrained.

propositions.name: Capital or the techno-economic process as machine intelligence
propositions.criterion: Capitalism, the market or the techno-economic process is itself an artificial or machine intelligence, or the process through which machine intelligence assembles itself.

propositions.name: Machine intelligence spreads beyond Earth
propositions.criterion: Machine intelligence will or could spread from Earth into space and through the universe, or convert the matter of the cosmos into intelligence.

propositions.name: Machine intelligence as a physical or cosmic process
propositions.criterion: The rise of machine intelligence is an expression of a physical, evolutionary or cosmological process larger than humanity (such as thermodynamics, the evolution of complexity or a cosmic destiny of intelligence).

propositions.name: The growth of intelligence as its own end
propositions.criterion: The increase of intelligence itself is the end that a sufficiently advanced intelligence pursues or should pursue, so that the final goals of advanced machine intelligence are not independent of its intelligence.

propositions.name: Machines succeed humans as the leading intelligence
propositions.criterion: Machine intelligence will or could replace or succeed human beings as the dominant or leading form of intelligence on Earth, or as the principal agent of further development, whether or not humans survive.

propositions.name: Human minds transferred into machines
propositions.criterion: A human mind could be transferred to, copied into or continued in a machine substrate, so that human beings could themselves become machine intelligences.

propositions.name: Conflict over building superhuman machines
propositions.criterion: Disagreement over whether superhuman machine intelligence should be built will divide human beings into opposed political groups, and could lead to large-scale war between them.

propositions.name: Succession by machines would be acceptable or desirable
propositions.criterion: The replacement or succession of human beings by machine intelligence (W01) would be acceptable, desirable or worth pursuing, for example because machines would be humanity's descendants or because the growth of intelligence matters more than its human form.

propositions.name: Superiority by many orders of magnitude
propositions.criterion: Machine intelligence could come to exceed human intelligence or overall cognitive capacity not moderately but by many orders of magnitude (a factor stated as trillions, or comparable to the gap between humans and much simpler organisms or matter). Capacity here means intelligence or overall cognitive capacity, not a robot's sensorimotor or output capacity.
